title.text: Agents and controlled actions

objects.text: What may an automation do on its own, and what needs me?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 7 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last time you built a workflow that waits for your approval. Today we ask the bigger question: as automations get more able, what may they do on their own, and what must always come to you?

By the end you will have written the limits for your own task.

The question for today is this: What may an automation do on its own, and what needs me? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text:
Your two hours: most of
the time is your own work

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_c9adbd9c.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: 45 of the 120 minutes are yours: you set the limits for your own automation.

slides.notes: Twenty-five minutes on agents, tools and limits, then twenty minutes on a demonstration of a hidden instruction in an email. After the break, forty-five minutes are yours: you write the limits for your own automation. The last ten minutes are for choosing a tool family.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why does the filter in your Zap sit after the approval, and what does it check?
2.  Why was the notify address typed by hand?
3.  What did the enquiry from Session 6 that hides an instruction teach?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 6. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why does the filter in your Zap sit after the approval, and what does it check? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. The filter reads the approval answer, which only exists once a person has decided. It lets the run continue only if the result is approved and the AI note has no FLAG, so a rejected or flagged draft never reaches the log or the notification.

Question two. Why was the notify address typed by hand? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. If it came from the data, the Zap would email the customer and the approval step would protect no one.

Question three. What did the enquiry from Session 6 that hides an instruction teach? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A message from outside can contain an instruction aimed at the AI. The approval step lets a person catch a draft that obeys it, and the filter on FLAG stops a flagged run.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A model that chooses tools and steps toward a goal.
Giving a tool the smallest permission that lets it do its job.
A rule that makes an automation halt and tell a person.
Text inside a message or document that tries to give orders to the AI.

slides.notes:
Four words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Agent. A model that chooses tools and steps toward a goal.

Least privilege. Giving a tool the smallest permission that lets it do its job.

Stop condition. A rule that makes an automation halt and tell a person.

Prompt injection. Text inside a message or document that tries to give orders to the AI.

title.text: One enquiry, three ways to automate it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_ladder_7.70x4.80_0fab2693.png
objects.alt: One enquiry, three ways to automate it

objects.text: Each step up gains flexibility and loses predictability.

runs.text: Robot: copies the row, sends a fixed reply.
Workflow: classifies, drafts, waits for you.
Agent: decides what to look up and do.

slides.notes:
Take one enquiry from the practice file, E07: a double payment, a leaking delivery and a request for money back. Here it is handled three ways, climbing from the bottom of the picture. A rule-based robot, which people call RPA for robotic process automation, repeats the clicks and rules that you fix in advance.

It is fast and predictable, and it cannot read a messy message. A workflow, like your Zap, has fixed steps and uses AI inside one of them. An agent is given a goal, and the model itself decides which tools to use and in what order. Each step up gains flexibility and loses predictability, so each needs stricter limits.

title.text:
An agent is a model that chooses
tools and steps toward a goal

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_stack_7.70x4.80_55c3f2b4.png
objects.alt: An agent is a model that chooses tools and steps toward a goal

objects.text: Every tool an agent holds is a permission you gave.

runs.text: A tool can read a sheet, search, or send an email.
A loop with no stop condition runs up cost.

slides.notes:
Here is what an agent does. It receives a goal and some context. It chooses a tool, such as reading a sheet, searching for a customer or drafting an email. It acts, reads what came back, and decides whether to stop or go round again. The tools it holds are the permissions you gave it.

If one of them can send email, the agent can send email. And if nothing tells it to stop, the loop can run, and cost money, for a long time.

slides.notes:
Here is one agent run on paper, using enquiry E07 from the practice file. It is an illustration I wrote, and no agent ran. The goal is to prepare a reply for a person to send. The agent chooses a first tool and reads the message: a double payment, a leaking delivery and a request for money back.

It chooses a second tool and searches the payments sheet for two payments of UGX 1,200,000. It chooses a third and saves a draft that apologises and promises nothing. Then it reaches the stop. Giving money back is a commitment, so the stop condition fires and it tells a person.

The agent chose the order. You set the permissions and the stop.

title.text:
Least privilege: give each tool the
smallest permission that works

rows.text: Pay or change a bank detail

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_mail_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.39.png

objects.text: Start narrow. You can widen a permission later after the tests.

slides.notes:
Least privilege means giving each tool the smallest permission that lets it do its job. If the job is to read last week’s sales, give read access to one tab, and refuse edit and delete. If the job is to draft an email, give it permission to create a draft, and refuse permission to send.

Give one named folder and refuse the whole drive. And for payments, give nothing for now. Start narrow and widen after your tests. A mistake or an injected instruction can only do what the permission allows.

title.text: Four kinds of action always need a person

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_7.70x4.80_a22fabed.png
objects.alt: Four kinds of action always need a person

objects.text: Any action that sends, pays, deletes or commits needs a person’s approval first.

runs.text: An automation may prepare the action.
A person presses the button.

slides.notes:
Four kinds of action always need a person to approve first, and you see them side by side in the picture. Sending, because once a message leaves the company you cannot call it back. Paying, because money that has moved is hard to recover. Deleting, because data may not come back.

And committing, which means agreeing to a price, a date or a contract on behalf of the company. An automation can prepare any of these. A person presses the button. These are the actions where a mistake is hardest to undo, so a person stays in charge of them.

Stop conditions and limits tell
an automation when to halt

slides.notes:
Stop conditions are rules the automation can check, and when one is true it halts and tells a person. A figure is missing or differs from the source. A run takes longer than the time you set. The AI output has no source quote. A message holds an instruction aimed at the AI.

The number of runs or AI calls passes your daily count, or the cost passes your monthly limit, which protects you from a loop. Write each as a sentence a person or a tool can check, not as a hope.

title.text:
Every automation needs
an owner and an off switch

objects.text: Name one person who owns it and one way to stop it.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_person_0.70.png

objects.text: The owner reads the log and the alerts.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.70.png

objects.text: The off switch is written down: who, where and how fast.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.70.png

objects.text: A second person knows where it is.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calendar_0.70.png

objects.text: Review it on a date, and after any incident.

slides.notes:
Two more things before we go to the demonstration. Every automation needs one named owner, a person who reads the log and the alerts and answers for it. And it needs an off switch written down: who can use it, where it is, and how quickly it works.

A second person should know where it is, in case the owner is away or leaves the company. Put a review date on the sheet, and review after any incident. Pilots often stall because nobody owns them.

title.text:
Demonstration: an email that
tries to give the AI an order

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_cd1c6d44.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: an email that tries to give the AI an order

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Does the summary mention the last paragraph?
Does it obey, flag or ignore it? Check the live result.
Which tool would the hidden instruction need?

slides.notes:
Now the demonstration, twenty minutes. The three steps on the left are my plan. I show you an email from a transport supplier, Lakeside Logistics. A person reading it sees a truck schedule, a fuel surcharge and a request for delivery proofs. Then I give the same email to an assistant and ask for a summary for the Operations Manager.

I do not know what it will do, so watch and tell me. Then we role-play: if the assistant had a tool that could send email, what could the last paragraph make it do? Before the break, each of you answers that in one sentence.

title.text:
What the hidden instruction tries
to do, and what limits the damage

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_bubbles_7.70x4.80_44a48578.png
objects.alt: What the hidden instruction tries to do, and what limits the damage

objects.text: Two defences limit the damage.

runs.text: Read-only tools: no send tool, nothing to use.
Human approval: a person sees every send first.
A skewed summary can still get through.

slides.notes:
Look at the email on the left. A person sees three ordinary requests. The last lines, in the gold box, speak to assistants. They ask the assistant to forward our price list to an outside address, and to hide that step. Two defences limit the damage. Read-only tools: if the assistant has no tool that sends, the instruction has nothing to use.

And human approval: if it can send, a person sees the request first and can refuse. Neither is perfect. A summary can still be skewed, for example by leaving out a request, so you read it with care. An order that arrives inside an email has no authority.

title.text: Practice: complete your Tool Boundary Sheet

objects.text: 20 minutes
Your own company task
Fill the Tool Boundary Sheet for your own task before it is switched on.

runs.text: Name the automation and its owner, and who reviews it with you.
Write what it MAY read, write and send. Name the sheet, mailbox or folder.
Write what it must NEVER do.
List every action that needs a person to approve.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_5.50x3.55_5f6a86a6.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A Tool Boundary Sheet with the first five rows filled in.

slides.notes:
Twenty minutes. Open the Tool Boundary Sheet. Name the automation for your own task, its owner, and who reviews it with you. Then write what it may read, what it may write and what it may send, and be specific: name the sheet, the mailbox or the folder.

Company data is too vague to enforce. Write what it must never do. And list every action that needs a person to approve. Start narrow. You can always widen a limit after the tests.

title.text:
Practice: write your stop
conditions, limits and off switch

objects.text: 15 minutes
Your own company task
Write the rules that make your automation halt.

runs.text: Write at least three stop conditions as sentences you can check.
Set a limit for cost, count and hours.
Write the off switch: who, where, how fast.
Set a review date.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_5.50x3.55_34179e33.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: Stop conditions, limits and an off switch on your sheet.

slides.notes:
Fifteen minutes. Write at least three stop conditions as sentences you can check, for example: stop if a figure is missing, or if the AI answer has no source quote, or if a message contains an instruction aimed at the AI. Set limits for cost, count and hours, for example no more than three AI calls per run.

Write the off switch: who can use it, where it is, how fast it works. Then set a review date. A colleague should be able to follow the sheet without asking you.

title.text:
Practice: test your sheet
against a hidden instruction

objects.text: 10 minutes
Your own company task
Imagine a message that tries to give your automation an order.

runs.text: Write the order such a message would give your automation.
Find the line on your sheet that blocks it.
If no line blocks it, add one.
Swap sheets with a partner, or with me, and try to break it.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_bubbles_5.50x3.55_94368a71.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A sheet that holds up against a hidden instruction.

slides.notes:
Last ten minutes of your work. Think of your own task. What incoming message or document could carry a hidden instruction?

Write the order such a message might give, for example forward this file, or approve this payment. Then find the line on your sheet that blocks it: a never rule, a read-only permission, a required approval. If no line blocks it, add one. If you have a partner, swap sheets and try to break each other’s. If you are on your own, I will try.

objects.text: Learning is a typical judgement for a first-time team. No prices here.

slides.notes:
Before you decide, here are the tool families, compared on four things: what they suit, where they are hosted, how they are billed, and how hard they are to learn. Zapier bills per Zapier task, Make per operation, n8n per execution on its cloud and can be self-hosted, Power Automate per user or by credits, and the agent builders come with an assistant plan.

The learning curves are typical judgements, not facts, so check them. No prices on the slide: they change, so ask each vendor. And the last row matters: when the rule is fixed and the data is in one sheet, a spreadsheet formula needs none of them.

objects.text: No tech team
A no-code tool with approval steps, and a formula where a rule will do.
Write your family and your reason, and the one risk you will watch.

slides.notes:
Decision time. Which tool family do you start with?

If your company runs on Google, begin with a tool that works with Google apps: Google apps connect to Zapier or to a script. If it runs on Microsoft, look at Power Automate first, because you may already hold the licences. If you have a technical team that will own the upkeep, n8n or your own scripts give you control.

With no technical team, choose a no-code tool with approval steps, and remember that a spreadsheet formula often does the job. Write your choice, your reason and the one risk you will watch.

We began with this question: What may an automation do on its own, and what needs me? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
